messages.subject: Access Posterior Distribution with Thinning
parts:
Dear RStanians,

Here is a problem I am not sure how to deal with after reading the post by the Stan team. I have a Stan model with simulation parameters set to the following:

######
parameters = c("b1", "b2", "b3", "b4", "b5", "b6", "b7", "thresh", "bmean", "bsigma", "log_lik")  # The parameter(s) to be monitored.
adaptSteps = 5000              # Number of steps to "tune" the samplers.
burnInSteps = 5000            # Number of steps to "burn-in" the samplers.
nChains = 3                   # Number of chains to run.

numSavedSteps=30000           # Total number of steps in chains to save.
thinSteps=10                  # Number of steps to "thin" (1=keep every step).
nPerChain = ceiling( ( numSavedSteps * thinSteps ) / nChains ) # Steps per chain.
######

Because this is a complex model for estimation and using shorter chains have failed to reach convergence, I am using a rather long chain with a thinning step set to 10 (save one iteration out of ten). Here I request to have 100,000 iterations for one chain, and only save one out of ten iterations for a total of three chains. It converged. Now my questions are:

1) How I can access only those saved steps? It looks like the extract() extracts all iterations, not those after thinning. So when I was trying to compare the descriptive statistics produced by summarizing across all iterations with those using pring(stan_fit), it's not surprising that they are different.

2) We can use the "generated quantities { }" block in stan to produce some post-estimation statistics using those means of estimated parameters and their credible intervals. I would assume we should be able to get the same results using the simulated posterior distributions. In this case, it should be the posterior after thinning, right?

Any thoughts? Thanks a lot!

Jun Xu, PhD
Associate Professor
Department of Sociology
Ball State University
Muncie, IN

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Access Posterior Distribution with Thinning
parts:
The argument for stan() in RStan is "thin", not "thinSteps".

Also, after the fact, you can pull out the draws and thin
there.

For (2), your description is not what happens. We don't
take the posterior mean and plug in, but rather do a full
Bayes computation.

So if you have

generated quantities {
real ealpha;
ealpha = exp(alpha);
}

alpha is some parameter, then for each draw for alpha, we compute
exp(alpha) and return the set of draws. Because exp isn't linear,
the answer won't be the same, because in general, if u is a vector,

exp(mean(u)) != mean(exp(u))

Jensen's inequality tells you which way it goes.

- Bob

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: Access Posterior Distribution with Thinning
parts:
On Monday, October 31, 2016 at 4:23:57 PM UTC-4, jun...@gmail.com wrote:
Dear RStanians,

1) How I can access only those saved steps? It looks like the extract() extracts all iterations, not those after thinning. So when I was trying to compare the descriptive statistics produced by summarizing across all iterations with those using pring(stan_fit), it's not surprising that they are different.

If you use the "thin" argument when calling the stan() function then afterwards extract should returned the thinned draws. For example 

library(rstan)
fit <- stan_demo(
  "eight_schools", 
  chains = 4, 
  iter = 200, 
  warmup = 100, 
  thin = 5
)
posterior <- extract(fit)
length(posterior$mu)

For this example length(posterior$mu) should be 4*(200-100)/5 = 80 post-warmup draws. Is that what you get if you run the code?

On another note, thinning is almost never a good idea. Running each chain for 100,000 iterations is very extreme (for Stan) and I would bet that there's a reparameterization of your model that would lead to much more efficient sampling. For some models that already use the most efficient parameterization you may still need a lot of iterations per chain but probably still an order of magnitude smaller than 100K. Regardless, thinning is just throwing away information. So unless you can't fit all the draws in memory or something like that I would avoid thinning.

2) We can use the "generated quantities { }" block in stan to produce some post-estimation statistics using those means of estimated parameters and their credible intervals. I would assume we should be able to get the same results using the simulated posterior distributions. In this case, it should be the posterior after thinning, right?

Maybe I'm misunderstanding what you mean, but you don't have access to posterior means and credible intervals inside the generated quantities block. The generated quantities block is run once per iteration, but posterior means and credible intervals require the full set of posterior draws and so can't be computed at each iteration. What you can do in generated quantities is compute functions of parameters using the value of the parameters at each iteration. Then after the fact you can get means and intervals for whatever you've defined in generated quantities.

Hope that helps,

Jonah

Thanks a lot to Jonah and Bob for answering my questions. I have to apologize that I made a couple mistakes while checking the results and didn't do a good job explaining my questions.

The problem related to my first question actually was caused by not specifying the "thin" option in my stan function, though I did specify the thinning parameter to be relayed to the thinning option outside the stan function. So here my question is whether the stan object contains posterior after thinning or before thinning. I guess Jonah already gave me the answer. It is the post-thinning posterior. But what if I want to have all iterations, including those dumped? Relatedly, which was probably answered by Jonah, is thinning a good idea to reach convergence. I wasn't able to reach convergence with a total of 100,000 iterations for three chains with thin set to 1. Convergence was not reached. I might be able to re-parameterize the model, which is complex and should be hard to estimate in theory. It was frustrating. So I increase the chain length with a large thinning number. So it is consensus that thinning is never a good idea?

Let me try to explain my second problem. Say we are to estimate a binary regression, and I also want to calculate the predicted probability of y=1 when all independent variables are set to their respective means. To calculate the prediction is straightforward, but its credible interval is not. One method we can use is to use generated quantities and calculate p(y=1) for each iteration, and once I get the posterior, I can simply get the 2.5% and 97.5% of p(y=1). Alternatively, I can put the posterior of all parameter estimates (of course iteration by iteration or vector by vector of parameters) into the inverse logit function, viz, exp(xb)/(1+exp(xb)), where x is given, and b is from each iteration of the posterior to get the distribution of predicted probability. My question is whether results from these two methods are equivalent. I would assume they are. Thanks a lot for all your help and sorry for my remiss.

Jun

> On Nov 3, 2016, at 3:05 PM, jun...@gmail.com wrote:

> Thanks a lot to Jonah and Bob for answering my questions. I have to apologize that I made a couple mistakes while checking the results and didn't do a good job explaining my questions.

So here my question is whether the stan object contains posterior after thinning or before thinning. I guess Jonah already gave me the answer. It is the post-thinning posterior. But what if I want to have all iterations, including those dumped?

If you have room to save them all, you should do that.
It'll give you better inferences (higher n_eff than
if you thin).
> Relatedly, which was probably answered by Jonah, is thinning a good idea to reach convergence.

No. Completely unrelated. We try to assess convergence by
running multiple chains and making sure they all get to
the same marginal means and standard deviations for each
parameter. That's what the R-hat stat does. Thinning won't
help with convergence.
> I wasn't able to reach convergence with a total of 100,000 iterations for three chains with thin set to 1. Convergence was not reached. I might be able to re-parameterize the model,

You will need to if you haven't converged. I don't
know what your model is, but this can be caused by
chains getting stuck at the same value due to
geometry (rarely, lowering step size and increasing adapt_delta
will help) or by their being alternative modes in which chains
get stuck (as in some kinds of mixture models) or by lack
of identifiability. See the manual chapter on problematic
posteriors.
> which is complex and should be hard to estimate in theory. It was frustrating. So I increase the chain length with a large thinning number. So it is consensus that thinning is never a good idea?

The only reason to thin is if you have long autocorrelations
and don't have enough memory to save all the draws. It
loses information, but saves space. If the autocorrelation gets
too long, then you need to reparameterize as all the estimates
of R-hat and n_eff may be off as they're very hard to estimate
at that range. In some cases like that, thinning may give the
illusion of convergence without actually having convergence, so
again, it's a bad idea.

> Let me try to explain my second problem. Say we are to estimate a binary regression, and I also want to calculate the predicted probability of y=1 when all independent variables are set to their respective means.

I take it the "independent variables" are what we call
"predictors" or "covariates"? And presumably they're
modeled if you're estimating population means? Or are
you just using sample means without any uncertainty?

> To calculate the prediction is straightforward, but its credible interval is not.


> One method we can use is to use generated quantities and calculate p(y=1) for each iteration, and once I get the posterior, I can simply get the 2.5% and 97.5% of p(y=1).
That's the Bayesian approach.

> Alternatively, I can put the posterior of all parameter estimates (of course iteration by iteration or vector by vector of parameters) into the inverse logit function, viz, exp(xb)/(1+exp(xb)), where x is given, and b is from each iteration of the posterior to get the distribution of predicted probability. My question is whether results from these two methods are equivalent. I would assume they are. Thanks a lot for all your help and sorry for my remiss.

They'd only be equivalent if the parameters were independent
and all the functions were linear.

- Bob

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: [stan-users] Re: Access Posterior Distribution with Thinning
parts: On Thursday, November 3, 2016, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> One method we can use is to use generated quantities and calculate p(y=1) for each iteration, and once I get the posterior, I can simply get the 2.5% and 97.5% of p(y=1).

That's the Bayesian approach.

> Alternatively, I can put the posterior of all parameter estimates (of course iteration by iteration or vector by vector of parameters) into the inverse logit function, viz, exp(xb)/(1+exp(xb)), where x is given, and b is from each iteration of the posterior to get the distribution of predicted probability. My question is whether results from these two methods are equivalent. I would assume they are. Thanks a lot for all your help and sorry for my remiss.

They'd only be equivalent if the parameters were independent
and all the functions were linear.

- Bob

I think I disagree with Bob here but it's probably because we're interpreting the question differently and not because there's an actual disagreement. You can always achieve the same thing you're doing in generated quantities after fitting the model using the full set of draws. Whether you compute P(y=1) inside generated quantities or after fitting the model shouldn't matter at all. What you don't want to do is to confuse computing intervals of a function with computing a function of the intervals. That doesn't give you the same thing except under strict conditions. 

Jonah
